passage.text: Dorothy watched her mother and grandmother adjust their hats in the mirror. The early morning light filtered through the curtains, softening their faces. Suddenly Dorothy saw Grandmother's eyes get watery.
"November 2, 1920. Now that this day has finally arrived, I can hardly believe it," Grandmother said, tears streaking her face.
"I know," Dorothy's mother answered, pulling Dorothy and Grandmother together into a hug.
Dorothy squirmed and looked at the clock. "Shouldn't we be leaving now, Mother?" she asked.

"Yes, Dorothy," her mother replied, smiling as she pulled on her good gloves, ready to go. Grandmother wrapped a new golden-yellow scarf around her neck and quickly patted her cheeks with face powder.
As they walked toward City Hall, Dorothy felt her cheeks flush from the cold air, excitement, or both. Grandmother was striding briskly, as if there were springs in her boots.

But when Dorothy saw the long line of people waiting outside the door to City Hall, her happiness turned to worry. The line snaked around the corner of the building and down the sidewalk. Hadn't her mother said that not everyone would welcome them in that line? In a panic, Dorothy imagined a City Hall worker locking the big brass doors and telling them they were too late. "Sorry," he would say, not sounding sorry at all. "Just come back in four years." She should have urged her grandmother and mother to hurry this morning!
Catching her eye, her grandmother asked, "Why the stormy face on such an important day, Dorothy?"

Now it was Dorothy's turn to get teary-eyed. "They aren't going to let us in," she whimpered. "There are so many people waiting in line." She sniffed and put her face in her hands, but she felt the immediate squeeze of a hug as her mother and grandmother put their arms around her from either side.
"They will, honey. We'll get in. You wait and see," said her mother. "The crowd is a good thing," she added, "because it shows that so many people care about this country."

"And we women are good at waiting, you know," Grandmother explained. "We've been determined and patient for so long, and today is our reward!" She paused, her face suddenly serious, and said, "We still have more work to do, though, if we want truly equal rights."

Dorothy remembered the many meetings her mother and grandmother had attended and all those rallies they'd marched in. For years, they had fought for the right to vote, and it was clear they would keep fighting. If they weren't anxious about being turned away, then Dorothy wouldn't be either.

She linked arms with her mother and grandmother, and they joined the end of the line. It was a cheerful group of women and men. The women greeted one another with hugs. The men smiled and nodded at the women, answering their questions about voting and chatting with them while they all waited together.
When they finally reached the entrance, her mother and grandmother signed their names and proceeded inside. Dorothy waited on a bench as the voters streamed in and out.
Spotting her mother and grandmother exiting, their heads held high, Dorothy threw her arms around them. "You did it!"
"We did it! We voted!" her grandmother said. "And soon, Dorothy, you will get to as well."

He loved making books and even loved sleeping in the shop's attic because it meant waking up to the smell of ink. Apprentices were in training, so they weren't paid. Ben felt rich, though, because he could read all the books that the shop printed. And not many fifteen-year-olds knew as much as he did about the printing business.
As Mr. Wilcox left, he said, "Oh, and Mr. Shakespeare is coming tomorrow."
William Shakespeare often came in to have his new plays printed in their shop. Ben loved Shakespeare's plays, especially the funny ones.

After quickly finishing his work, Ben rushed to meet his brother, Jamie. They got together most weeks when they each had a half-day off. Jamie was apprenticed to a London shoemaker, but he didn't aspire to be one himself. His real desire was to become an actor.

Ben met Jamie at their usual spot. Today Jamie was making his voice sound like the shoemaker's. "No, young Jamie," he croaked. "You haven't used nearly enough shoe polish. If your hands don't stink of polish for days, you're doing it wrong!"
"I'm sorry you don't like making shoes," Ben answered between chuckles. Jamie always made him laugh.
"I want to leave every day!" Jamie said. "Let's become actors together—you love plays, right?"
"Well yes, but…"

"No buts, brother," Jamie interrupted. "Follow me!" Jamie took off running down a narrow alley, with Ben wondering where they were going and hurrying to keep up. Soon he spotted Jamie's destination: the Globe Theater, where Shakespeare's company performed.
"Tickets are cheap today, so let's go!" Jamie exclaimed. The play was As You Like It. The boys stood in the back and joined in the loud laughing and hooting and clapping.

As the show ended, Jamie said, "Let's find out how to join!" He tugged Ben toward the crowd of actors behind the stage, pushing forward to talk with them. Meanwhile, Ben hung back from the crush of people. Soon, Jamie rejoined Ben, moaning, "It's really hard to get a place here unless you know somebody."

Ben knew it would be several years until they finished being apprentices, and they'd get into trouble if they left before their apprenticeships were up. Also, he'd miss Mr. Wilcox and his printing press. But Jamie had made up his mind that they would join the theater together, and Jamie never took no for an answer. Finally, Ben promised he'd work on an "escape plan."

The next morning, Ben still didn't have a plan and wondered what he'd tell Jamie. Then, the shop door opened. "Mr. Shakespeare!" Ben exclaimed, his voice squeaking slightly. That's when he had his idea.

A week later, Ben ran to meet his brother waving a letter. "I talked to William Shakespeare about you, about how talented and funny you are, and look at this. He wants to see you! He says the company needs a new boy!"
Jamie jumped up and hugged Ben, exclaiming, "But we're joining together, right?"
"We can't all be on stage, Jamie. Someone has to print the plays, and someone has to watch them. I'll be with you," Ben said, "cheering in the stands."

title.text: When the Ludds Got a Microwave

passage.text: Michelle Ludd was kneading dough with her father to make his special cheese bread when the front door swung open. Mrs. Ludd staggered into the house, her arms wrapped around an enormous cardboard box.
"What on earth is this?" Michelle's father asked, taking the box from Mrs. Ludd and heaving it onto the kitchen table.
"I won a prize at work," Mrs. Ludd explained, "for selling the most houses for the company in 1984. I have no idea what's in that box, but it better be something wonderful."

Michelle found the scissors and carefully cut open the package. Inside, wrapped in thick padding, was a shiny new microwave oven. Looking disappointed, Mr. Ludd patted his wife's shoulder. "We could donate it," he suggested, as Mrs. Ludd nodded her head. "The Good Deeds Soup Kitchen is always asking people to help out by giving kitchen items," he added.
"But wait, these things are amazing!" Michelle protested. "A microwave oven can cook an entire meal in minutes!"
Her mother waved a hand in the air, declaring, "There's already too much rushing in the world."
Mr. Ludd told a story about watching TV with some friends and seeing an ad for a microwave. "We all joked about how microwaves waste your counter space to do exactly what a stove already does."
"It's like these new video games," Mrs. Ludd added. "What's going to happen to board games? Goodbye, family time!"

Michelle sighed. She should have known. When Michelle had suggested they buy a VCR, her parents had seemed puzzled. After she explained that the VCR was a machine that could record and play television shows, her parents just looked at each other and laughed.

Michelle slid her palm across the top of the microwave. "You could at least use it to warm up your leftover coffee," she said. She knew how much her parents despised cold coffee. They refused to drink it.
Mr. Ludd tilted his head, thinking. "That's not a bad point," he said.
"I suppose we could stick it in the far corner next to the stove," Mrs. Ludd said.
And that's what they did. Michelle's parents used the microwave to heat up their leftover coffee, but other than that, the machine sat unused.
Then one evening, all three Ludds came home worn out from their busy days. Michelle had run in her track meet, her mother had worked late, and her father had been running errands all day.
"I was planning to make baked potatoes for dinner," Michelle's father said, "but they'll take an hour to bake."

Her mother groaned, and Michelle realized this was her chance. She opened the drawer where she had saved the booklet of directions that came with the microwave. Flipping to the correct page, she looked up and announced, "We could microwave the potatoes in minutes."
"Really?" Mr. Ludd asked, reading the instructions over her shoulder. "All right then; let's give it a whirl."
Fifteen minutes later, they sat down to baked potatoes loaded with cheese and green onions.
"Delicious," said Michelle's mother.
"Technology has its perks," mused her father.

Michelle smiled and sprinkled some more shredded cheese on her potato. "Maybe we can play a board game after dinner," she said with a playful grin. "After all, it's still early enough for family time."

passage.text: "Oh no!" Emma gasped, peeking outside into the gloomy Vermont afternoon. "It's snowing!"
"Oh my, what a summer! That awful snowstorm in June, frost in July, and now snow again in August," Mama replied. "Our corn is done for sure."
Emma sighed and said, "I hear people are calling 1816 'The Year Without a Summer.'"
"Ha," Mama said, shivering and moving to add some wood to the fire in the fireplace. "More like 'Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death.'"

Emma hurried outside to fill the kettle with water, and then she set it to boil over the fire. She thought of their corn crop freezing in the fields. Their garden hadn't produced much either. They were lucky to have a stash of last year's root vegetables in the cellar.
"I'm hungry, Mama," cried her little brother Zeke.
"It's still a while until supper," Mama said. "But you can have this potato while you wait."
"We have potatoes every day!" Zeke complained. Emma shot him a look and he quieted, accepting the warm potato that Mama scooped from the fireplace coals.
"I'm fresh out of new ways to cook beets and potatoes," Mama told Emma softly.
Emma was out of new ideas herself. She needed some air. "I'll check on Buster," she said, pulling on her coat and boots.

She tramped out to the barn and greeted the old brown horse. Buster snorted and stamped in the stall. "At least we have lots of oats for you," Emma observed, scooping some into Buster's bucket. They also had plenty of maple syrup, which they'd boiled down from sap a few months back.

Emma's thoughts swirled as she considered supper. She didn't think she could stand yet another meal of beets and potatoes. She'd heard that nettle flowers were good to eat if you boiled them. Emma was willing to try them, but she wasn't up for going nettle-picking until this snow melted.

Buster's oats reminded her of something, though. Hadn't Granny May told her about eating oats during hungry times? At the time, she'd thought Granny was telling one of her tall tales. Emma didn't know anybody who ate oats. But what if they could?
Emma scrambled up the barn ladder to the loft where old family treasures were stored. Where was Granny's box?
A few moments later, Emma burst into the house with new vigor, waving her grandmother's recipe box. She did a little dance and announced, "I'll cook tonight—and it won't be root vegetables!"
"Yay!" Zeke cried.

With a bag from the barn and a jar from the cellar, a little of this and a little of that, Emma worked busily about the kitchen fire. When Mama went out to pump more water, Zeke whispered to Emma, "Is that horse food?"
Emma whispered back, "It's Granny May's special recipe."
When they finally sat down to plates loaded with the results of her work, Emma waited nervously as Zeke and Mama took their first bites.
"Delicious!" Zeke said, grinning.
"Wonderful!" Mama agreed.
"It's Granny May's maple oatmeal cakes," Emma said with relief.
"I think this recipe needs a new name," Mama said with a smile. "How about 'Emma's Special Oat Cakes'?"
"Let's have them every night!" Zeke added.

passage.text: I bet I could help, too, if given the chance, Susanna thought as she chopped wood at her family's Virginia farm.

The sixteen-year-old girl had been thinking about how proud she was of her father, who was away with George Washington's army. Susanna admired all the different ways that people in the American colonies were supporting the fight for independence.
She stopped chopping wood when shouts and hoofbeats caught her ear. Dropping her axe, she peeked out the woodshed window and gasped to see a swarm of red-coated soldiers—the British!
Susanna ran in the back door of their house and heard someone banging loudly on the front door. "They don't sound happy," Mother observed.

No doubt the British were unhappy, Susanna thought. They'd just lost a battle against Lafayette, the young French general who was fighting on the American side. She'd heard that General Lafayette was staying at the Half Way House Inn, fifteen miles away.

"Wait in the kitchen," Mother said, heading to open the front door. Susanna obeyed, and soon Mother joined her there. "That's the British general, Cornwallis," she whispered to Susanna. "He wants supper tonight for the troops he's leading, so we have work to do."

That evening when Susanna served the officers their supper, they were deep in a serious discussion and continued their talk, ignoring her. Then, she heard Cornwallis announce, "We'll attack them from the rear, surprise them, apprehend Lafayette, and win this war."
Susanna felt dizzy with worry. Lafayette was in danger of being caught!
As she cleared the plates and washed the dishes, Susanna wondered how she might ask a neighbor to warn Lafayette. Then it hit her: she could do it. She dried her hands and made a plan.
It was after midnight when Susanna crept outside through the darkness to the river's edge. She pulled her canoe from the bushes but froze when a stern voice shouted, "Who's there?"
After a moment, the soldier muttered, "Must have been a raccoon." As his footsteps faded away, Susanna took a deep breath, and then she slid her canoe into the water.

She paddled to the Smith farm on the far bank. The Smiths were friends and wouldn't mind her borrowing their horse for her errand. Susanna saddled a sleepy mare and hopped on, her heart fluttering. If the British caught her, they'd throw her in jail, or worse!
Luckily, the road was empty, and Susanna reached the Half Way House easily. She led the horse around to the back and threw open the inn's kitchen door.
Stepping inside, Susanna immediately grabbed two copper kettles and banged them together: CLANG! The innkeeper's wife came running at the noise and let out a shriek when she saw Susanna.
"Please, ma'am," Susanna gasped, holding out both hands. "I'm Susanna Bolling. I have an important message for General Lafayette!"
More people hurried into the kitchen, including a young man in uniform. "You are looking for me?" he asked, in an unfamiliar accent. Suddenly, Susanna couldn't speak.
"What message for Lafayette, Mademoiselle?"
Finally, Susanna's tongue came unstuck. "An attack—to capture you!" Then she told Lafayette about overhearing Cornwallis's plan.
He listened, nodded, and said, "You have done me—and your country—an important service. Excuse me, I have much that I must do." He bowed and left, shouting directions to his men.
I knew I could help, thought Susanna, grinning.

passage.text: The crowded boat rolled in the water, and Ling was filled with a mixture of dread and excitement. He'd spent the last six weeks stuck in Angel Island Immigration Station in San Francisco Bay, with many others who had sailed from China to the United States. Finally, the U.S. officials said they were satisfied that Ling was indeed the son of Wong Lee, an American citizen. At last, he was heading to meet Father, who waited for him at the San Francisco pier.

Ling shivered, more from nervousness than from the cold. He closed his eyes, trying to picture his father's face. It was four years since Father had left Ling with Grandmother and sailed for San Francisco. Two months ago, Ling's father had sent him the ship ticket with a note saying Ling could join him now.

Now that Ling himself had taken the same trip from China, his mind drifted to the stories he had heard from an older boy on the ship. The boy had called the city "Gold Mountain," telling Ling that anyone could find golden rocks there and become rich. Even though his father hadn't described his life, Ling figured he must have made a fortune in four years.

Now the boat bumped against a dock, and the American boatman shouted something that Ling didn't understand. But Ling grabbed his small bag and jumped onto the dock, eagerly scanning the faces in the crowd. Was Father here?
Suddenly a man approached, shouting, "Ling!" Though his memory of his father's face was hazy, Ling knew that voice.
"Father!" Ling replied, leaping into his father's arms and ignoring the stares of the people around them.
"Let's go, son," his father urged. "I'll show you San Francisco."
They walked for quite a while. This place didn't look like Gold Mountain to Ling. He stopped in front of a wrecked building. "What destroyed this place?" he asked with dismay.
"There was a terrible earthquake seven years ago, in 1906," Father explained. "They are still fixing some places. Soon we will have a new city hall here, better than before."

Before long, they entered streets lined with tall buildings and stores selling Chinese goods. Signs everywhere were written in Chinese characters that Ling recognized. He looked around, breathing in the smells of fresh-caught fish and special teas. The place before him was both familiar and foreign.

There was no gold, though, other than gold paint on some of the storefronts and buildings. The clothes Ling's father wore, though clean, looked old and worn. Ling frowned. "Where should we dig for gold, Father?"
His father laughed and said, "Ling, my son, I don't dig for gold. Where did you get that idea? I own a market where I sell fruits and vegetables."
Ling asked, "So I'll work in the store?"
"Here," said Father, "you will go to school."
School? School sounded good. Back home, they didn't have enough money for school.

"And next year, after we save more money," Father continued, "we'll make a new start." He explained how friends of his had been talking about creating a new Chinese town outside of the city, along the Sacramento River. He thought they'd do well in such a place.

Ling's dream of a golden house with many servants melted away. But he heard the excitement in his father's voice, and a new dream formed in Ling's mind. He pictured this new village where he and Father would make their fine new home and he would go to school.
Father said, "Ling, I'm sorry we are not rich with gold."
Ling shrugged and then answered, "Father, I think we are rich in many things."
